title: Authorization Rate: What It Is and How to Increase Payment Approval Rates
summary: Learn what payment authorization rate means, how to calculate it, why transactions get declined, and proven ways to improve approvals, routing, retries, and checkout performance.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


Not every payment attempt results in a successful transaction. A customer may have sufficient funds and still face a decline because of issuer-bank checks, incorrect transaction data, authentication issues, fraud controls, routing problems, or temporary technical failures.


This is where authorization rate becomes an important payment performance metric. It measures the percentage of eligible payment authorization attempts that receive approval. For ecommerce businesses, subscription platforms, travel companies, fintechs, and other digital businesses, even a small improvement in authorization rate can help recover legitimate transactions, increase completed orders, and reduce lost revenue.


##


**What Is Authorization Rate?**


Authorization rate, also called payment approval rate, is the percentage of eligible payment authorization attempts that are approved.


The basic formula is:


**Authorization Rate = (Approved Authorization Attempts ÷ Total Eligible Authorization Attempts) × 100**


For example, if a business submits 1,000 eligible card payment attempts for authorization and 920 are approved:


**(920 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 92%**


An authorization rate of 92% means that 92 out of every 100 eligible authorization attempts received approval.


The exact calculation can vary depending on the payment provider and reporting methodology. Businesses should therefore use a consistent definition when comparing authorization performance over time or across payment providers.


##


**Authorization Rate vs Payment Success Rate**


Authorization rate and[payment success rate](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/what-is-payment-success-rate/) are related, but they measure different stages of the payment journey.


**Metric** **What It Measures**


Authorization rate Percentage of eligible payment authorization attempts that receive approval


Payment success rate Percentage of payment attempts that successfully complete the payment journey


Decline rate Percentage of eligible authorization attempts that are declined


Capture rate Percentage of authorized payments that are successfully captured


A payment can receive authorization but still fail to complete because of an issue during capture, confirmation, or subsequent processing.


For India-focused businesses, this distinction is particularly important. Card authorization rate should be monitored separately from UPI transaction success rate, net banking success rate, wallet success rate, and other payment-method-specific metrics.


### **First-Attempt vs Recovered Authorization Rate**


Businesses should also distinguish between payments approved on the first attempt and payments recovered after an initial failure.


First-attempt authorization rate measures the percentage of eligible payment attempts approved during the initial authorization attempt.


A separate recovery rate can show how many initially failed but eligible payments were subsequently recovered through an approved recovery mechanism.


Tracking these separately prevents retries from masking a weak first-attempt payment experience.


##


**Why Does Authorization Rate Matter?**


A low authorization rate can mean that legitimate customers are being declined even when they are willing and able to complete a purchase. At scale, these false declines can result in lost revenue and lower[checkout conversion](https://www.cashfree.com/one-click-checkout/) .


Improving authorization rates can help businesses:


- Recover legitimate transactions that would otherwise be declined.
- Increase completed orders and checkout conversions.
- Reduce payment-related customer complaints.
- Improve[recurring payment collection](https://www.cashfree.com/recurring-payment/) and reduce involuntary churn.
- Identify underperforming issuers, payment routes, payment methods, or fraud rules.
- Make better decisions about payment gateways, acquirers, routing strategies, and fraud controls.


However, a higher authorization rate should not come at the expense of payment security. Businesses should aim to maximize legitimate approvals while maintaining appropriate fraud and chargeback controls.


##


**Why Do Businesses Have Low Authorization Rates?**


Before attempting to improve authorization rates, businesses need to understand why payments are failing. Declines can result from customer, issuer, merchant, fraud, or technical and routing issues.


### **Declines Due to Customer-Related Issues**


Customer-related declines occur when the customer’s account or payment method prevents the transaction from being approved.


Common causes include:


- Insufficient funds or available credit
- Expired cards
- Incorrect card details
- Cards not enabled for online or ecommerce transactions
- Transactions exceeding applicable cardholder or issuer limits
- Authentication failures


Some of these declines cannot be recovered through routing or retries. Providing customers with clear error messages and alternative[payment methods](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-mode-types/) can help them complete the purchase without repeatedly attempting the same failed payment.


### **Declines Due to Issuer-Bank Issues**


An issuer-bank decline occurs when the issuing bank does not approve a transaction based on factors such as the customer’s account status, transaction history, risk assessment, or internal policies.


Examples include:


- The issuer suspects potentially fraudulent activity.
- The transaction does not match the cardholder’s usual spending behaviour.
- The card is not enabled for ecommerce or[international transactions](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/how-to-receive-international-business-payments-in-india/) .
- The issuer is temporarily unavailable.
- Additional authentication or verification is required.
- The transaction exceeds an issuer-defined limit or restriction.


Some issuer declines may be temporary and potentially recoverable, while others should not be retried.


### **Declines Due to Merchant or Transaction Data Errors**


Incomplete, inaccurate, or incorrectly formatted transaction data can prevent an issuer or payment processor from properly evaluating a payment request.


Depending on the payment flow, relevant information can include:


- Transaction amount and currency
- Merchant information
- Customer and billing information, where applicable
- Card verification information
- Card-on-file and recurring-payment indicators
- Authentication information
- Order, shipping, or transaction context where relevant


Businesses should also verify that payment fields are correctly mapped across their checkout, payment gateway, processor, and internal systems.


Even a small data-mapping error can result in avoidable payment failures.


### **False Positives From Fraud Rules**


Fraud prevention is essential, but overly restrictive fraud rules can block legitimate customers. This is known as a false positive.


For example, a business may have rules that automatically decline:


- High-value orders
- All first-time purchases
- Foreign-issued cards
- Multiple attempts from the same customer
- Transactions from certain locations or devices


If too many legitimate transactions are blocked before they can be properly evaluated, checkout conversion can suffer.


Businesses should regularly review fraud-rule performance alongside[chargebacks](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/chargebacks-meaning-how-they-works-types-causes-prevention/) , fraud outcomes, manual-review results, and approval rates. The objective is to identify rules that create unnecessary declines without materially reducing fraud.


### **Declines Due to Technical and Routing Failures**


Temporary technical problems can also affect payment performance. These may include:


- [Payment gateway](https://www.cashfree.com/payment-gateway-india/) or processor downtime
- Connectivity problems
- Slow response times
- Route-specific failures
- Poor performance for a particular payment method
- Capacity issues during traffic spikes
- Acquirer or processor outages


Intelligent payment routing can help reduce some of these failures by directing eligible transactions through better-performing configured routes.


However, routing cannot override a genuine issuer decision. For example, changing the route will not guarantee approval when a card is declined because of insufficient funds or suspected fraud.


##


**How to Increase Payment Authorization Rates**


Improving authorization rates requires a combination of payment data analysis, transaction optimization, fraud management, checkout improvements, and payment infrastructure.


### **1. Track the Right Payment Data**


The first step is to establish a reliable baseline. Do not look only at your overall authorization rate. Break performance down by:


- Payment method
- Issuer bank
- Card network
- Debit and credit cards
- Domestic and international transactions
- Transaction value
- New and returning customers
- One-time and recurring payments
- Device type
- Gateway, processor, acquirer, or payment route
- Geography
- Day, time, and campaign period


This segmentation can reveal where declines are concentrated.


For example, a business may have a healthy overall card authorization rate but discover that one issuer or payment route performs significantly worse during peak evening traffic.


### **2. Analyse Decline Reasons**


Declines should not be treated as one generic failed-payment category. Businesses should classify declines into groups such as:


- Hard declines
- Soft or temporary declines
- Fraud-related declines
- Authentication failures
- Technical failures
- Customer-abandoned payments


Hard declines, such as invalid or blocked payment credentials, generally should not be retried.


Some temporary or technical failures may be recoverable through an appropriate retry or alternative payment route.


A clear decline-code framework helps payment teams determine which failures are potentially recoverable and which should not be retried.


### **3. Improve Transaction Data Quality**


Payment requests should contain accurate, complete, and correctly formatted information. Businesses should review whether their payment flows correctly pass:


- Merchant information
- Transaction amount and currency
- Relevant customer and billing information
- Card verification data where applicable
- Authentication information
- Card-on-file indicators
- Recurring-payment indicators
- Other relevant transaction context


For[recurring payments](https://www.cashfree.com/recurring-payment/) , businesses should also verify that customer consent, tokens, mandates, and applicable recurring-payment markers are correctly maintained and passed through the payment flow.


Improving data quality can help reduce avoidable declines and give payment partners and issuers better transaction context.


### **4. Use Tokenisation for Saved Cards**


[Card tokenisation](https://www.cashfree.com/card-tokenization/) replaces sensitive card details with a secure token.


For customers, tokenisation can make repeat payments easier because they do not need to enter their card details each time.


For businesses, tokenized payment flows can reduce payment friction and support safer saved-card experiences. Where supported by the payment ecosystem, network tokenization and account-updater capabilities can also help maintain payment credentials when cards are reissued or updated.


Subscription businesses, ecommerce brands with returning customers, and platforms using saved-card checkout can benefit from well-designed tokenized payment flows.


### **5. Use Smart Payment Routing**


[Smart payment routing](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/smart-payment-routing/) allows businesses to direct eligible transactions through suitable configured payment routes based on factors such as payment method, issuing bank, transaction type, geography, recent route performance, and business-defined rules.


Instead of sending every transaction through a single fixed route, businesses can use routing logic to select a better-performing route for a particular payment scenario.


Smart routing can be especially useful for businesses that:


- Process high transaction volumes
- Use multiple gateways or acquirers
- Experience issuer- or payment-method-specific failures
- Run large sales or ticket launches
- Experience significant traffic spikes
- Need greater visibility into route-level payment performance


Smart routing does not guarantee approval. Its value is in reducing avoidable failures associated with route availability, performance, or suitability.


### **6. Create Intelligent Retry Rules**


Retries can recover some eligible soft or temporary failures, but they should be used carefully. A retry strategy should define:


- Which decline types are eligible for retry
- How long to wait before retrying
- How many retries are permitted
- When to stop retrying
- When to notify the customer
- How to verify the payment’s latest status before initiating another attempt


For example, a temporary technical failure may justify a retry after an appropriate interval. An invalid card or suspected fraud decline generally should not simply be retried.


Businesses must also follow applicable card-network, issuer, acquirer, and regulatory requirements when implementing retry logic.


Blindly retrying every failed payment can increase duplicate-payment risk, create customer frustration, and potentially violate payment-network rules.


### **7. Optimise Authentication Without Creating Excess Friction**


Authentication and authorization are related but different stages of a payment. Authentication helps establish that the customer is authorized to use the payment instrument, while authorization determines whether the transaction can be approved. Businesses should ensure that authentication is triggered correctly and that customers receive clear instructions throughout the process. The authentication experience should also work smoothly across mobile and desktop devices.


For card payments, businesses should implement applicable authentication and security measures in accordance with relevant regulatory and card-network requirements.


The goal is to maintain strong security while avoiding unnecessary friction that could cause customers to abandon checkout.


### **8. Review Fraud Rules Regularly**


Fraud controls should prevent genuinely risky transactions without unnecessarily blocking legitimate customers.


Businesses should review:


- Fraud rules with high decline rates but limited fraud prevention impact.
- Customer segments that are frequently blocked but rarely generate chargebacks.
- Transactions sent for manual review and subsequently approved.
- False positives related to transaction value, location, device, or velocity.
- Changes in fraud and chargeback rates after rule updates.


A well-calibrated fraud strategy can help businesses improve authorization and conversion while maintaining an acceptable risk profile.


### **9. Offer Alternative Payment Methods**


Not every customer prefers to pay by card. In India, businesses can offer payment methods such as:


- [UPI](https://www.cashfree.com/upi-payment-gateway/)
- Net banking
- Wallets
- EMI
- [Pay Later options](https://www.cashfree.com/buy-now-pay-later/)
- Cards


Offering relevant alternatives can improve overall payment conversion, although it does not directly increase card authorization rate.


For example, if a customer’s card payment fails, providing a convenient UPI option can help recover the sale without requiring the customer to retry the same card.


### **10. Optimise Recurring Payment Flows**


Recurring payments can fail for several reasons, including expired or updated card credentials, insufficient funds, authentication issues, or inactive mandates.


Businesses collecting subscriptions, premiums, instalments, memberships, or recurring invoices should:


- Use tokenized credentials where supported.
- Maintain valid mandates and customer consent records.
- Send payment reminders before due dates.
- Use clear dunning communication after failed payments.
- Give customers a simple way to update payment details.
- Provide alternative payment methods where appropriate.


The optimization approach also depends on the payment method. Card subscriptions, for example, can involve tokenized credentials, while[UPI recurring payments](https://www.cashfree.com/upi-autopay/) depend on valid mandates and applicable UPI rules.


A well-designed recovery strategy can reduce involuntary churn, where customers want to continue using a service but their payment fails.


##


Measuring and Improving Authorization Rate Over Time


Authorization optimization is an ongoing process rather than a one-time project. Businesses should monitor payment performance regularly, identify changes in decline patterns, and test optimization strategies in a controlled manner.


### **Metrics to Monitor**


**Metric** **Why It Matters**


Authorization rate Shows the share of eligible authorization attempts that receive approval


First-attempt authorization rate Shows how many eligible payments succeed on the initial authorization attempt


Decline rate Helps identify the volume and pattern of failed authorization attempts


Payment success rate Shows whether payments successfully complete the end-to-end journey


Retry recovery rate Measures eligible failed payments recovered through retries


Route-level success rate Identifies better- and worse-performing payment routes


Fraud decline rate Helps identify potential false positives in fraud controls


Chargeback rate Ensures higher approvals are not creating excessive payment risk


Checkout conversion rate Shows the broader impact of payment performance on completed orders


##


**First-Attempt vs Recovered Payments**


Businesses should track first-attempt authorization performance separately from recovered payments.


If retries are included without clear reporting, the overall payment rate may appear healthier while hiding a weak first-attempt experience.


Separating these metrics helps businesses understand:


- How many payments succeed on the first attempt.
- How many soft or temporary failures are subsequently recovered.
- Whether retries are improving revenue without creating unnecessary friction.
- Which payment methods or transaction segments require deeper optimization.


##


**Illustrative Example: D2C Checkout Optimisation**


A[D2C brand](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/how-indian-d2c-brands-can-win-more-nri-customers/) notices that its card authorization rate falls during flash sales.


The payment team reviews transaction data and finds that failures are concentrated on one payment route during high-traffic periods.


The business responds by:


1. Introducing smart routing for eligible transactions.
2. Monitoring route-level performance during peak traffic.
3. Reviewing fraud rules that were blocking a high number of first-time customers.
4. Making UPI more visible as an alternative payment method.


As a result, more eligible card transactions can be directed through better-performing routes, while customers who cannot complete a card payment have an alternative way to pay.


The important point is that authorization optimization is not about forcing every transaction through a successful authorization. It is about identifying legitimate transactions that can be approved while maintaining appropriate fraud and risk controls.


##


**A Practical 90-Day Authorization Rate Optimization Plan**


Businesses looking to improve payment authorization rates can use the following framework.


### **Days 1–30: Diagnose**


- Establish baseline authorization and payment success rates.
- Separate first-attempt and recovered payments.
- Segment declines by issuer, payment method, route, transaction type, geography, and value.
- Identify the most common decline reasons.
- Audit transaction, authentication, and recurring-payment data quality.


### **Days 31–60: Optimise**


- Fix missing or incorrectly mapped transaction fields.
- Review fraud rules for false positives.
- Improve authentication and checkout messaging.
- Make relevant alternative payment methods easier to access.
- Configure smart routing or improve route-level performance monitoring.
- Create a compliant retry strategy for eligible temporary failures.


### **Days 61–90: Test and Scale**


- Run controlled tests on routing, retry timing, fraud rules, and checkout flows.
- Compare first-attempt and recovered payment performance.
- Monitor authorization gains alongside fraud and chargeback outcomes.
- Identify the highest-impact payment segments.
- Scale successful optimization strategies across additional transaction volumes.

##


Conclusion


Authorization rate measures the percentage of eligible payment authorization attempts that receive approval. It is an important payment-performance metric because authorization outcomes can affect revenue, checkout conversion, customer experience, and recurring collections.


To improve payment authorization rates, businesses should analyse decline reasons, maintain accurate transaction data, use tokenisation where appropriate, review fraud controls, optimise authentication, apply intelligent payment routing, build compliant retry strategies, and offer relevant payment alternatives.


The goal is not simply to approve more transactions. The goal is to recover legitimate payments that should have succeeded while keeping fraud, chargebacks, and customer friction under control.


##


**FAQs**


#### **What is authorization rate in payments?**


Authorization rate is the percentage of eligible payment authorization attempts that receive approval. It is generally calculated by dividing approved authorization attempts by the total eligible authorization attempts and multiplying the result by 100.


#### **How do you calculate authorization rate?**


Use this formula:


```text
Authorization Rate = (Approved Authorization Attempts ÷ Total Eligible Authorization Attempts) × 100
```


For example, if 920 out of 1,000 eligible authorization attempts are approved, the authorization rate is 92%.


#### **What is a good payment authorization rate?**


There is no single authorization rate that can be considered good for every business. Performance varies based on factors such as industry, payment method, customer geography, transaction value, issuer mix, fraud profile, and payment infrastructure.


Businesses should benchmark authorization performance across their own payment methods, issuers, routes, and transaction segments rather than rely on a single industry-wide number.


#### **What causes payment authorization failures?**


Payment authorization failures can result from insufficient funds, incorrect payment details, expired cards, issuer risk decisions, authentication failures, merchant-data errors, fraud controls, technical problems, or payment-route failures.


#### **How can businesses increase payment authorization rates?**


Businesses can improve authorization rates by analysing decline reasons, improving transaction data quality, optimizing authentication, using tokenisation where appropriate, reviewing fraud rules, implementing suitable payment routing, using compliant retry strategies, and monitoring payment performance by issuer, route, payment method, and transaction type.


#### **Does smart payment routing improve authorization rates?**


Smart payment routing can help reduce route-related payment failures by directing eligible transactions through better-performing or more suitable payment routes. However, routing cannot override genuine issuer declines caused by factors such as insufficient funds or suspected fraud.


#### **Should businesses retry declined payments?**


Not every declined payment should be retried. Businesses should distinguish between potentially recoverable temporary failures and declines that should not be retried. Retry strategies should also comply with applicable card-network, issuer, acquirer, and regulatory requirements.


#### **What is the difference between authorization rate and payment success rate?**


Authorization rate measures whether an eligible payment authorization attempt is approved. Payment success rate measures whether the payment successfully completes the broader payment journey. A payment can therefore be authorized but still fail later in the payment process.
